t:
Sec. 211. 

(a) 
Effective June 30, 1996, the functions of the  Comptroller General identified in subsection (b) are transferred to the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, contingent upon the additional transfer to the Office of Management and Budget of such personnel, budget authority, records, and property of the General Accounting Office relating to such functions as the Comptroller General and the Director jointly determine to be necessary. The Director may delegate any such function, in whole or in part, to any other agency or agencies if the Director determines that such delegation would be cost-effective or otherwise in the public interest, and may transfer to such agency or agencies any personnel, budget authority, records, and property received by the Director pursuant to the preceding sentence that relate to the delegated functions. Personnel transferred pursuant to this provision shall not be separated or reduced in classification or compensation for one year after any such transfer, except for cause.


(b) 
The following provisions of the United States Code contain the functions to be transferred pursuant to subsection (a): sections 5564 and 5583 of title 5; sections 2312, 2575, 2733, 2734, 2771, 4712, and 9712 of title 10; sections 1626 and 4195 of title 22; section 420 of title 24; sections 2414 and 2517 of title 28; sections 1304, 3702, 3726, and 3728 of title 31; sections 714 and 715 of title 32; section 554 of title 37; section 5122 of title 38; and section 256a of title 41.



Sec. 212. 

(a) 
Section 732 of title 31, United States Code, is amended by adding a new subsection (h) as follows:


“(h) 
Notwithstanding the provisions of subchapter I of chapter  35 of title 5, United States Code, the Comptroller General shall prescribe regulations for the release of officers and employees of the General Accounting Office in a reduction in force which give due effect to tenure of employment, military preference, performance and/or contributions to the agency’s goals and objectives, and length of service. The regulations shall, to the extent deemed feasible by the Comptroller General, be designed to minimize disruption to the Office and to assist in promoting the efficiency of the Office.”.






Sec. 213. 
Section 753 of title 31, United States Code, is amended—

(1) 
by redesignating subsections (b), (c), and (d) as (c), (d), and (e), respectively;



(2) 
by inserting after subsection (a) a new subsection (b) as follows:


“(b) 
The Board has no authority to issue a stay of any reduction in force action.”; and





(3) 
in the second sentence of subsection (c), as redesignated, by striking “(c)” and inserting “(d)”.

fable.w: Section 212 requires the Comptroller General to prescribe regulations, and the definition counts a requirement or authority to make rules as participation. The tempting opposite reading is that the section is purely internal: it transfers functions between GAO and OMB and governs GAO personnel, so every actor is inside the federal government. That reading has real force, because these are internal personnel rules that may not involve public comment, but the explicit rulemaking mandate tips the label to Yes.
fable.s: the Comptroller General shall prescribe regulations for the release of officers and employees of the General Accounting Office in a reduction in force

qwen_block.w: This section describes the internal reorganization of the federal government, specifically transferring functions and personnel between the General Accounting Office and the Office of Management and Budget. Both entities are part of the federal government, so this is intra-governmental coordination, not participation by outside parties. There is no mention of consultation with states, the public, or other non-federal entities.
qwen_block.s: Effective June 30, 1996, the functions of the Comptroller General identified in subsection (b) are transferred to the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, contingent upon the additional transfer to the Office of Management and Budget of such personnel, budget authority, records, and property of the General Accounting Office relating to such functions as the Comptroller General and the Director jointly determine to be necessary.

opus.w: Sec. 212 requires the Comptroller General to issue regulations. Under the definition and Example 6, requiring or authorizing rulemaking counts as participation. The tempting "No" reading is that the rest of the section is purely internal: functions move between federal agencies, and a Board loses the power to stay layoffs. But that reading overlooks the rulemaking mandate. Some doubt remains because these are internal personnel rules of a legislative-branch agency, which may be exempt from public comment.
opus.s: the Comptroller General shall prescribe regulations for the release of officers and employees of the General Accounting Office in a reduction in force which give due effect to tenure of employment, military preference, performance and/or contributions to the agency’s goals and objectives, and length of service.
opus.b:
I'm labelling this Yes, with moderate confidence (about 0.6). It turns on the regulation-writing provision in Sec. 212.

The tempting reading is "No." Sec. 211 moves functions from the Comptroller General to the Director of the Office of Management and Budget and lets the Director pass them to other agencies. Sec. 213 strips a Board of the power to stay reduction-in-force actions. Everyone involved in both sections is inside the federal government, and the regulations in Sec. 212 cover only the General Accounting Office's (GAO's) own staff layoffs.

But the definition counts "requiring rulemaking" as "Yes." Example 6 also treats any statutory authority to issue regulations as participation. Sec. 212 requires the Comptroller General to issue regulations, so under that rule the answer is "Yes."

The confidence is moderate because the GAO is a legislative-branch agency, and internal personnel rules are often exempt from public notice-and-comment. In practice, no outside party may ever take part.

qwen_chat.w: This section describes the transfer of functions and personnel between federal agencies (GAO and OMB) and the delegation of authority within the executive branch. It does not involve consultation or coordination with any parties outside the federal government, such as states, tribes, or the public. The actions described are purely internal administrative adjustments.
qwen_chat.s: The functions of the Comptroller General identified in subsection (b) are transferred to the Director of the Office of Management and Budget... The Director may delegate any such function... to any other agency or agencies
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the "Board" mentioned in Sec. 213 is an advisory body involving outside parties, or that the transfer of functions involves consultation. However, the text describes internal administrative changes within the federal government (transferring functions between the GAO and OMB, prescribing regulations for federal employees, and limiting the authority of an internal board). There is no mention of consulting with states, tribes, the public, or other non-federal entities. The "Board" referred to is likely the Merit Systems Protection Board or an internal GAO board, which are federal entities. The definition explicitly excludes intra-government coordination and reports to Congress.
